function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “starter kit” you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repo.  
It contains:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a minimal Node JS image |
| `k8s.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/docker-image.yml` | CI that builds & pushes the image to GHCR |
| `.dockerignore` | Keeps the build context lean |

> **NOTE** – The repo you mentioned (`git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`) is assumed to contain a simple Express/Node app that listens on port **3000** (the most common default).  
> If your app uses a different port or entry point, adjust the files accordingly.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – Alpine gives a small footprint
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why node:18‑alpine?**  
> * Alpine is lightweight, and Node 18 is the LTS version at the time of writing.  
> If you prefer a different Node version, change the `FROM` line accordingly.

---

## 2. Kubernetes YAML (`k8s.yaml`)

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
# ------------------------------------
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # Change to ClusterIP / NodePort if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 2 replicas of your app.  
> * Exposes the container’s port 3000 to the cluster.  
> * Creates a LoadBalancer service that forwards external traffic on port 80 to the pods.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow (`.github/workflows/docker-image.yml`)

```yaml
# .github/workflows/docker-image.yml
# ------------------------------------
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Docker Buildx (multi‑arch support)
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      - name: Login to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build & push the image
      - name: Build & push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

> **How it works**  
> 1. Triggered on every push to `main`.  
> 2. Builds the image from the `Dockerfile`.  
> 3. Pushes the image to **GitHub Container Registry** under the same name as the repo (`ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome`).  
> 4. Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication – no extra secrets required.

---

## 4. Optional: `.dockerignore`

```text
# .dockerignore
node_modules
npm-debug.log
Dockerfile
.dockerignore
.git
.gitignore
.github
```

> Keeps the Docker build context small.

---

## 5. Add, Commit & Push

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo (if you haven’t already)
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome

# 2. Add the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/docker-image.yml .dockerignore

# 3. Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 4. Push to main
git push origin main
```

> After the push, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the image, and push it to GHCR.  
> You can verify the workflow status in the **Actions** tab of the repo.

---

### Quick sanity check

1. **Build locally** (optional):  
   ```bash
   docker build -t nodejs-welcome:latest .
   docker run -p 3000:3000 nodejs-welcome:latest
   ```
   Visit `http://localhost:3000` to confirm the app is reachable.

2. **Deploy to a cluster** (optional):  
   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
   ```
   Then check the service:  
   ```bash
   kubectl get svc nodejs-welcome-service
   ```

That’s it! Your repo now has a production‑ready Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a CI pipeline that keeps your container image up‑to‑date whenever you push to `main`. Happy coding!
